The Stoics offered the standard formula: beauty is the symmetry of parts with one another and with the whole, together with a pleasing colour. Plotinus, in the third century CE, attacked this directly and made a decisive move. If beauty were proportion, he argued, only composite things could be beautiful, yet a single colour, a flash of lightning, a pure tone and the sun are beautiful without having parts to be proportionate. Moreover a face can retain its proportions and lose its beauty. Plotinus concluded that beauty is the shining of form, of intelligible order, through matter, and that we recognise it because our soul is akin to it. This is the source of the long-lived notion that beauty is a kind of radiance rather than a measurement.

Medieval thought synthesised these positions within a theological frame. Augustine held that beauty resides in unity, number and order, all reflecting the divine, and that we love beautiful things because they participate in God's beauty. Thomas Aquinas, in the thirteenth century, gave the most influential formula: three things are required for beauty, namely integritas or wholeness, since defective things are ugly; consonantia or due proportion; and claritas, brightness or clarity, the shining forth of a thing's form. He also defined the beautiful as that which pleases upon being seen, id quod visum placet, a formula that anticipates modern accounts by locating beauty in a relation between object and perceiver rather than in the object alone.

The proportion tradition left a durable practical legacy: the golden ratio of approximately 1.618, systems of architectural orders, the canon of human proportions, and the rule of thirds in composition. Its evidential status is weaker than its cultural presence suggests. Empirical studies of preference for golden-ratio rectangles, running from Gustav Fechner in the 1870s onward, have produced inconsistent results, and the widespread claim that the Parthenon and the Great Pyramid were designed on it is largely a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sections.heading: The Eighteenth Century Turn: Taste, and Hume's Standard
sections.body:
In the eighteenth century the centre of gravity shifted from the object to the subject. The question stopped being what makes things beautiful and became what happens in us when we find them so. The key term was taste, understood as an inner sense that responds to beauty as the palate responds to flavour.

Francis Hutcheson, in 1725, proposed an internal sense of beauty that operates immediately and involuntarily, and offered a formula: beauty is proportional to uniformity amidst variety. Shaftesbury emphasised disinterested contemplation, the idea that aesthetic appreciation involves setting aside any desire to possess or use the object. Joseph Addison's Spectator essays on the pleasures of the imagination popularised the discussion for a broad public.

The subjective turn creates an obvious difficulty. If beauty is a response in us, it seems to follow that all responses are equally correct, and that nothing more can be said. David Hume confronted this directly in his essay Of the Standard of Taste in 1757, and his treatment remains the standard starting point.

Hume begins by conceding the sceptical position entirely. Beauty, he says, is no quality in things themselves; it exists merely in the mind which contemplates them, and each mind perceives a different beauty. Every sentiment is right, because sentiment refers to nothing beyond itself. But he immediately notes that this conclusion collides with practice. Whoever asserted an equality of genius between the seventeenth-century hack John Ogilby and Milton would be thought to defend an extravagance as absurd as maintaining a molehill to be as high as a mountain. Our actual judgements are not egalitarian.

His resolution is to seek the standard not in the object but in the qualified judge. Some critics, he argues, are better instruments than others, and their joint verdict constitutes the standard. He specifies five characteristics: delicacy of taste, the capacity to discriminate fine differences, which he illustrates with a story from Don Quixote in which two kinsmen detect a faint taste of leather and of iron in a hogshead of wine and are vindicated when a key on a leather thong is found at the bottom; practice, since repeated exposure to a genre sharpens perception; comparison, the experience of many works and degrees of quality; freedom from prejudice, setting aside one's own circumstances to occupy the position the work addresses; and good sense, the ability to grasp the work's design and the consistency of its parts.

The obvious objection is circularity: we identify good critics by their agreeing with our judgements of good works, and good works by the agreement of good critics. Hume's defenders reply that the criteria are independently specifiable and empirically testable, and that convergence over time among experienced judges is evidence, not definition. Hume himself concedes two irreducible sources of variation that no standard removes: the different humours of particular persons, and the manners and opinions of particular ages.

sections.heading: Kant and the Judgement of Taste
sections.body:
Immanuel Kant's Critique of the Power of Judgment, published in 1790, is the most influential single work in aesthetics, and its central problem is precisely the tension Hume identified. Kant wants to explain how a judgement can be based purely on subjective feeling and yet legitimately claim that everyone ought to agree.

He analyses the judgement of taste, the judgement that something is beautiful, under four headings borrowed from his table of categories. Under quality, the judgement is disinterested. When I judge a rose beautiful, I am not interested in whether it exists, whether I own it, whether it is useful, or whether it satisfies any desire. Kant sharply distinguishes this from the agreeable, which is bound up with sensory gratification and private inclination, and from the good, which involves a concept of what the thing ought to be. A judgement of beauty is a wholly free and contemplative pleasure.

Under quantity, the judgement is universal but subjective. Because I am aware that my pleasure does not rest on any private interest, I speak as though beauty were a property of the object and demand assent from others. Kant's formulation is that beauty is what pleases universally without a concept. This is the crux: I cannot cite a rule or produce a proof, because there are no determinate concepts of beauty. If someone recites a hundred critics in favour of a poem, Kant says, I stop my ears and judge for myself.

Under relation, beauty is purposiveness without purpose, Zweckmässigkeit ohne Zweck. The beautiful object appears designed, its parts fitting as if for an end, yet we attribute no actual purpose to it. Under modality, the judgement claims necessity of a special kind, resting on the presupposition of a common sense, a sensus communis, a shared capacity for the relevant response.

The mechanism Kant proposes is the free play of the faculties. Ordinary cognition works by the imagination gathering a sensory manifold and the understanding subsuming it under a concept. In aesthetic experience the imagination presents a form that suits the understanding's demand for unity without any particular concept being applied. The two faculties fall into a harmonious, self-sustaining play, and the feeling of that harmony is aesthetic pleasure. Because the faculties are the same in all rational beings, the pleasure can be demanded of everyone.

Kant distinguishes free beauty, such as flowers, arabesques and instrumental music, judged with no concept of what the thing should be, from dependent beauty, such as a church or a horse, judged partly against a concept of its kind. He also introduces genius as the talent through which nature gives the rule to art, producing original works that are exemplary and whose rules the artist cannot state. Later aesthetics inherits from Kant the ideas of disinterestedness, autonomy of art, and the aesthetic attitude, all of which twentieth-century critics would attack.

sections.heading: The Sublime: Beauty's Difficult Companion
sections.body:
Alongside beauty, eighteenth-century writers isolated a second aesthetic category, the sublime, which covers experiences that are overwhelming, even terrifying, and yet valued. Storms at sea, alpine precipices, vast deserts, thunder, the starry sky: none of these are pretty, and all of them move people profoundly.

The idea descends from a Greek treatise, On the Sublime, traditionally ascribed to Longinus and probably written in the first century CE, which discusses the power of great writing to transport rather than merely persuade an audience. Rediscovered and translated by Boileau in 1674, it was reworked into a theory of natural experience.

Edmund Burke's A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful of 1757 gave the first systematic empirical account. Burke traces the two categories to two primary human drives. Beauty belongs to the social passions and arises from qualities that produce love: smallness, smoothness, gradual variation, delicacy, clear and mild colours. The sublime belongs to self-preservation and arises from whatever excites the ideas of pain and danger: vastness, obscurity, power, privation, infinity, loudness, suddenness. Crucially, the sublime requires distance. Actual danger produces simple terror; danger contemplated from safety produces what Burke calls delight, a negative pleasure consisting in the removal of pain. His mechanism is physiological, a tension of the nerves that exercises the finer parts of the system, an account which is quaint but which anticipates modern research on benign masochism, the enjoyment of controlled distress in horror films, hot chillies and roller coasters.

Kant reworked the sublime in idealist terms and divided it in two. The mathematically sublime arises when we confront magnitude that defeats imagination's capacity to take it in as a whole, such as the pyramids seen too close or the night sky. The imagination strains and fails, but that very failure awakens the idea of infinity in reason, and we feel our supersensible vocation as rational beings. The dynamically sublime arises from overwhelming natural power, such as volcanoes, hurricanes and the boundless ocean, contemplated in safety; nature reveals our physical insignificance, but simultaneously we recognise that our moral personality is not subject to natural force. For Kant the sublime is therefore not in nature at all but in the mind's discovery of its own superiority, and the feeling is a complex of momentary check followed by outpouring.

The sublime shaped Romantic art profoundly, from Caspar David Friedrich's tiny figures before mountain seas to Turner's storms, and it re-entered twentieth-century discussion through Jean-François Lyotard, who took it as the characteristic modern aesthetic mode: the attempt to present the fact that the unpresentable exists. It also names an important truth: aesthetic value is not confined to pleasantness, and the most powerful artistic experiences are often disturbing.

sections.heading: What Is Art? Imitation, Expression, Form
sections.body:
By the nineteenth century the mimetic definition of art was failing. It never fitted architecture or instrumental music well, and Romanticism made the misfit obvious by treating art as the outpouring of an inner state rather than the copying of an outer one. Three families of definition contended.

The expression theory holds that art is the communication or embodiment of emotion. Its blunt form is Leo Tolstoy's, in What Is Art? of 1897: art is a human activity in which one person consciously hands on feelings they have lived through, by means of external signs, so that others are infected by these feelings and also experience them. Tolstoy drew radical conclusions, judging sincerity and universal accessibility to be the marks of good art and dismissing most of the European canon, including his own novels, as elite entertainment. The theory's difficulty is that it collapses art into effective emotional transmission, which propaganda and advertising achieve superbly, and it cannot explain works that are subtle, ironic or deliberately cold.

R. G. Collingwood's The Principles of Art of 1938 offers a far more sophisticated version. He distinguishes art proper from craft, which is the skilled achievement of a preconceived end, and from amusement and magic, which arouse emotion for a purpose. Art proper is the expression of emotion, and Collingwood means something specific: the artist begins with an unarticulated disturbance and, through the act of making, comes to know what it is. Expression is therefore not transmission of a known feeling but the clarification of an unknown one, and the work is essentially imaginative, the physical object being a means by which an audience reconstructs the artist's imaginative experience.

Formalism moves in the opposite direction, locating value entirely in the arrangement of perceptible elements. Clive Bell, in Art of 1914, coined significant form, the particular combination of lines and colours that stirs a distinctive aesthetic emotion, and insisted that nothing about the subject matter, the artist's biography or the emotions depicted is relevant. This was an argument for Post-Impressionism against Victorian narrative painting, and it was polemically effective. Its weakness is circularity: significant form is defined as what produces aesthetic emotion, which is defined as what significant form produces. Eduard Hanslick had made a musical version in 1854, arguing that the content of music is tonally moving forms and nothing else.

Each theory illuminates part of the field and fails elsewhere. Formalism handles abstract painting and absolute music and stumbles on literature and conceptual art. Expression theory handles lyric poetry and stumbles on architecture. Mimesis handles portraiture and stumbles on ornament. This repeated pattern of partial success suggested to some philosophers that the search for a single defining essence was itself the error.

sections.heading: The Anti-Essentialist Challenge and the Institutional Theory
sections.body:
In 1956 Morris Weitz published a paper arguing that art cannot be defined at all, and it changed the direction of the field. Drawing on Ludwig Wittgenstein's discussion of games in the Philosophical Investigations, Weitz argued that art is an open concept. Wittgenstein had observed that games share no common feature; board games, ball games, card games, solitaire and ring-a-ring-o'-roses form a family with overlapping and criss-crossing similarities, like the resemblances among members of a family, and no single thread runs through all. Weitz claimed art is the same, and moreover must be, because the concept must remain open to accommodate genuine innovation. A closed definition would rule out in advance the next unforeseen kind of work, and creativity guarantees such works keep arriving.

The argument had force, but it also had a glaring problem: by the mid-twentieth century artists were producing objects with no perceptible features distinguishing them from ordinary things. Marcel Duchamp's Fountain of 1917, a mass-produced urinal signed R. Mutt and submitted to an exhibition, is the canonical case. Andy Warhol's Brillo Boxes of 1964, plywood replicas of supermarket cartons, made the point sharper still: two objects can be perceptually identical while one is art and one is a shipping carton. Whatever makes the difference is not visible.

Arthur Danto responded in 1964 with the idea of an artworld: to see something as art requires something the eye cannot descry, an atmosphere of artistic theory and a knowledge of the history of art. Later, in The Transfiguration of the Commonplace of 1981, he argued that artworks are about something, embody a meaning, and require interpretation against an art-historical context.

George Dickie developed this into the institutional theory of art. In its refined form, a work of art is an artefact created to be presented to an artworld public, where the artworld is the totality of artworld systems and an artist is a person who participates with understanding in making a work. The definition is deliberately procedural rather than evaluative: it says how something becomes art, not whether it is any good. Critics complain of circularity, since every term is defined by the others, and of emptiness, since it seems to say art is whatever the art establishment accepts, which invites the charge that the theory sanctifies fashion.

Alternative approaches persist. Historical definitions, associated with Jerrold Levinson, hold that something is art if it is intended for regard in some way that prior artworks were correctly regarded, making arthood a matter of lineage. Cluster accounts, defended by Berys Gaut, list a set of criteria such as possessing positive aesthetic qualities, being expressive of emotion, being intellectually challenging, being the product of skill, and belonging to an established art form, and hold that satisfying enough of them suffices without any being necessary.

sections.heading: Aesthetic Properties, Perception and the Role of Knowledge
sections.body:
Beneath the definitional disputes lies a quieter and arguably more tractable question: what are aesthetic properties, and how do we come to perceive them?

Aesthetic properties are those such as elegant, graceful, garish, balanced, moving, delicate, unified, insipid, dynamic, sentimental and serene. They differ from ordinary descriptive properties such as being red, weighing two kilograms, or containing seven figures. Frank Sibley, in an influential 1959 paper, argued that aesthetic concepts are not condition-governed: no set of non-aesthetic descriptions entails an aesthetic conclusion. There is no rule saying that any painting with these colours in this arrangement is garish. Applying aesthetic terms requires taste, an exercise of perceptiveness rather than the application of a criterion. Yet, crucially, aesthetic properties depend upon non-aesthetic ones; nothing could change its elegance without some underlying change in line, proportion or colour. This relation, dependence without entailment, is what philosophers call supervenience, and it is one of the more secure results in the field.

Whether aesthetic properties are genuinely in objects or are responses in us remains contested. Realists point out that we correct each other, that expertise exists, that a person can fail to see the balance in a composition and later come to see it, which suggests something was there to be seen. Anti-realists reply that the same is true of secondary qualities like colour, which are relational, and that aesthetic properties are response-dependent: to be elegant is to be disposed to elicit a certain response in appropriately situated observers. This is a sophisticated middle position, making aesthetic properties real but constitutively tied to human sensibility, in the way that being nauseating is real without being independent of creatures who feel nausea.

A further question concerns how much knowledge is needed. Kendall Walton's 1970 paper Categories of Art argued powerfully that aesthetic perception is category-relative. A work perceived as belonging to a category has standard features, which are characteristic of the category, variable features, which vary within it, and contra-standard features, which tend to disqualify it. Flatness is standard for painting and contra-standard for sculpture. Walton's thought experiment imagines guernicas, a hypothetical genre of works whose surfaces have varying relief; Picasso's Guernica seen as a guernica would appear cold, static and unemotional rather than violent, because its flatness would be a variable feature and its shapes would read as barely departing from the norm. The same physical object has different aesthetic properties depending on the category correctly assigned to it.

This has a substantial consequence: aesthetic perception is not innocent looking. It is informed looking, saturated with historical knowledge about what kind of thing is being perceived. The apparent immediacy of aesthetic response conceals a great deal of learned classification.

sections.heading: Interpretation, Intention and the Meaning of Works
sections.body:
A large part of what critics do is interpret, and a persistent question is what constrains interpretation and whether the artist's intentions settle meaning.

The debate was sharpened by W. K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley's 1946 essay The Intentional Fallacy, which argued that the design or intention of the author is neither available nor desirable as a standard for judging the success of a literary work. Their case has several strands. The poem is a public object made of language, and its meaning is determined by that language, not by a private mental event. Intentions are frequently unavailable, and where available may be unreliable, since artists misremember and rationalise. Most decisively, if the intention succeeded, it is realised in the work and we do not need to consult it; if it failed, we should not credit it. The essay underwrote the New Criticism, with its close reading of the text as a self-sufficient verbal icon.

Anti-intentionalism has clear limits. Irony, allusion, parody and satire are unintelligible without some grasp of what the maker was doing. A random pattern in sand produced by waves may look like a poem but means nothing; the same shapes produced deliberately mean something. Meaning seems to require an agent.

The modern positions therefore cluster in the middle. Actual intentionalism holds that a work means what its maker intended, provided the words or materials can bear that meaning. Hypothetical intentionalism, defended by Levinson, holds that a work means what an ideally informed audience of its time would most reasonably take the artist to have intended, which preserves the role of agency without making a private mental fact decisive. Beardsley's own later position was that works have meanings independent of their makers, fixed by conventions plus context.

Beyond the intention question, twentieth-century theory multiplied approaches: psychoanalytic readings after Freud, Marxist readings attending to the work's relation to production and class, structuralist readings mapping underlying codes, and the deconstructive readings of Jacques Derrida which sought internal instabilities in texts. Roland Barthes' 1967 essay The Death of the Author declared the birth of the reader to be at the cost of the death of the author, arguing that meaning is produced in reading rather than deposited by writing.

Against interpretive proliferation, Susan Sontag's 1964 essay Against Interpretation argued that the modern habit of translating art into content, of asking what a work means rather than attending to how it is, impoverishes experience. Her closing line, that in place of a hermeneutics we need an erotics of art, is a plea to restore sensuous attention. The tension she names is real, and any serious criticism has to hold both: works reward interpretation, and interpretation can substitute for the encounter it was meant to serve.

sections.heading: Aesthetic Value, Pleasure and Why Art Is Good For Us
sections.body:
Suppose we agree a work is good. What is it good for, and what kind of value is aesthetic value?

The simplest account is hedonic: aesthetic value is the capacity to produce a certain kind of pleasure. This is old and durable, and it captures why we return voluntarily to works. Its difficulty is well known. Some outstanding works are gruelling rather than pleasant; people watch Bergman and read Primo Levi without anything easily called enjoyment. Moreover the pleasure account seems to license the experience machine objection: if pleasure is all that matters, a drug or a machine producing the same pleasure would be as valuable as the work, which almost nobody accepts. This suggests we value the specific engagement, not just the resulting state.

Cognitivists argue that art has genuine epistemic value: it teaches. Not usually in the form of propositions, though novels do convey information, but by providing detailed imaginative acquaintance with situations, moral possibilities and forms of life. Martha Nussbaum has argued that certain moral truths, particularly about particularity and emotional perception, can only be adequately expressed in narrative form, so novels are not illustrations of philosophy but a mode of philosophical work. Sceptics reply that fiction's claims are untested, that a vivid falsehood teaches falsehood equally well, and that any beliefs acquired are unjustified because the author simply stipulated the world.

A third family locates value in what the engagement does to us. Aesthetic experience exercises perception, imagination and empathy; it trains attention. Some evidence supports modest versions of this: reading literary fiction has been associated in several studies with small improvements in tests of theory of mind, though replication has been mixed and effect sizes are small. Honesty requires saying that grand claims about art making people better have thin empirical support and considerable counter-evidence, most starkly the cultured cruelty of the twentieth century.

The relation between aesthetic and moral value is itself a live debate. Autonomism holds that a moral defect in a work is aesthetically irrelevant; a beautifully made propaganda film is beautifully made. Moralism holds that moral defects are always aesthetic defects. Berys Gaut's ethicism offers a moderate version: a work's manifested attitudes, where morally flawed, are to that extent aesthetically flawed, because the work prescribes responses that are unmerited and the audience is entitled to refuse them. Leni Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will is the standing test case, and even those who admire its technique generally concede the admiration is uncomfortable in a way that pure formalism cannot explain.

A useful distinction, finally, is between aesthetic value and artistic value. A cathedral, a novel and a chess problem may all be beautiful, but artistic value plausibly includes originality, historical significance, technical achievement and depth of engagement with a tradition, none of which is straightforwardly perceptual.

sections.heading: Beyond the Western Canon: Other Aesthetic Traditions
sections.body:
Almost everything described so far is European, and treating that tradition as aesthetics itself is a serious distortion. Other traditions have developed sophisticated theories that pose questions the Western tradition barely asks.

Classical Indian aesthetics centres on rasa, meaning flavour or juice, systematised in the Natyashastra attributed to Bharata, compiled somewhere between the second century BCE and the second century CE. The theory holds that a performance evokes in the audience an impersonal, savoured emotional essence. Eight rasas were canonical, the erotic, comic, pathetic, furious, heroic, fearful, odious and marvellous, with tranquillity added later as a ninth. Each corresponds to a durable emotion in the spectator, awakened through a combination of determinants, consequents and transitory states. The eleventh-century Kashmiri philosopher Abhinavagupta developed the crucial point: rasa is not the ordinary emotion but a generalised, depersonalised relishing of it, freed from self-interest, which is why grief in drama is savoured rather than suffered. This is a genuinely different solution to the paradox of tragedy from Aristotle's catharsis, and arguably a subtler one. Anandavardhana's theory of dhvani, suggestion, holds that the highest poetic meaning is what is suggested rather than stated.

Chinese aesthetics developed around qi yun sheng dong, the spirit resonance and life-movement named as the first of Xie He's six principles of painting in the sixth century. The painter's task is not to reproduce appearance but to convey the vital energy of the subject, and calligraphy, poetry and painting are understood as a single family of practices expressing the cultivated character of the maker. The literati tradition explicitly valued the amateur scholar-artist over the professional craftsman, inverting a Western hierarchy.

Japanese aesthetics contributed a distinctive vocabulary of terms with no European equivalents. Mono no aware, the pathos of things, names the poignant awareness of transience that makes cherry blossom moving precisely because it falls. Wabi-sabi values imperfection, roughness, asymmetry and the marks of age and use, an aesthetic of the weathered and incomplete visible in tea ceremony ware and in kintsugi, the repair of broken pottery with gold so the fracture becomes the ornament. Yugen names a profound, mysterious suggestiveness. Ma is the significant interval, the charged emptiness between forms.

Islamic aesthetic traditions, shaped by a general avoidance of figural representation in religious contexts, developed geometry, arabesque and calligraphy to extraordinary sophistication, with the endless repeating patterns of tilework understood by many commentators as an evocation of divine infinity.

These traditions are not merely different tastes. They embody different accounts of what art is for, and they suggest that some Western commitments, autonomy of art, the artwork as a discrete object, the separation of art from craft and from ritual, are local rather than universal.

sections.heading: Modern Challenges: Conceptual Art, Everyday Aesthetics and the Environment
sections.body:
The twentieth and twenty-first centuries generated problems that classical aesthetics was not built for, and the field has expanded to meet them.

Conceptual art, from the 1960s onward, made the idea the work and the physical realisation optional. Sol LeWitt's 1967 sentences declared that the idea becomes a machine that makes the art, and that the execution is a perfunctory affair. Works consisting of instructions, certificates, gestures or documentation strain any perception-based account of aesthetic value; if the work is the concept, aesthetic experience in Kant's sense may be entirely absent. Some philosophers conclude that art and the aesthetic have simply come apart, so that a definition of art cannot proceed via beauty at all. Others argue that conceptual works still offer a distinctive experience, one of intellectual apprehension with its own satisfactions.

Performance and time-based art raise ontological puzzles about what and where the work is. A symphony is not identical with any performance or score; a dance may exist only in bodies and memory; digital works may depend on obsolete hardware. Philosophers distinguish singular works, like a painting, from multiple works, like a novel or an etching, and debate whether the latter are types with performances as tokens.

Everyday aesthetics, developed by writers including Yuriko Saito and Thomas Leddy, argues that confining aesthetics to art was a mistake that cut philosophy off from most of aesthetic life: the appearance of a meal, the tidiness of a room, the feel of a well-worn tool, the sound of rain on a roof, the choreography of a commute. These experiences are pervasive, they shape wellbeing and behaviour, and they have moral dimensions, since caring how things look and feel is bound up with care for others and for the world.

Environmental aesthetics recovered a subject that dominated the eighteenth century and then nearly vanished. Ronald Hepburn's 1966 essay revived it by observing that natural appreciation differs structurally from art appreciation: nature is unframed, we are inside it, it engages all senses, and it has no author whose intentions guide us. Allen Carlson argues for scientific cognitivism, holding that appreciating nature properly requires knowing what one is looking at, so that geology and ecology play the role art history plays for paintings, and that a wetland appreciated as a swamp is misappreciated. Others defend a role for imagination, emotion and mystery. The stakes are practical, since conservation arguments frequently rest on aesthetic claims, and the picturesque tradition of valuing scenery has demonstrably distorted land management toward views rather than ecosystems.

Empirical aesthetics, meanwhile, has grown into a serious research programme, using psychology and neuroimaging to study preference, fluency, arousal and expertise, with findings such as the reliable preference for moderate complexity and for prototypical exemplars. Whether such findings answer philosophical questions or merely describe the responses philosophy seeks to evaluate is itself disputed.

sections.heading: Persistent Problems and Honest Uncertainties
sections.body:
Several problems in aesthetics have resisted solution long enough that their persistence is itself philosophically interesting, and a fair account should present them as open.

The paradox of tragedy asks why we seek out representations of suffering. Hume's essay Of Tragedy proposed that the pleasure of eloquence converts the painful passions, so that the distress heightens rather than diminishes overall enjoyment. Modern accounts include compensation, the idea that pleasures of form and understanding outweigh the distress; conversion theories; control theories, noting that the emotion is chosen and can be ended; and meta-response theories, holding that we take pleasure in finding ourselves the kind of person who is moved. None is decisively established.

The paradox of fiction asks how we can be genuinely moved by people we know do not exist. Colin Radford's 1975 formulation argued our responses are irrational, since emotion normally requires belief in the object's existence. Kendall Walton replied that what we feel are quasi-emotions within a game of make-believe, and that we do not literally fear Dracula but make it fictional that we do. Thought theorists respond that vividly entertaining a thought suffices for emotion without belief, which most now find the least strained option.

The paradox of taste, Hume's and Kant's shared problem, remains genuinely unresolved. We have no good account of how a judgement can be at once irreducibly first-personal and legitimately normative. Every proposal, ideal critics, sensus communis, response-dependence, secures one horn at some cost to the other.

Other open questions abound. Whether an artwork's moral flaws are aesthetic flaws is contested with serious philosophers on both sides. Whether forgeries are aesthetically inferior to originals when perceptually indistinguishable, raised sharply by Nelson Goodman, splits opinion; Goodman argued that merely knowing two pictures differ can make a perceptual difference matter, since it directs future looking. Whether there is a distinctive aesthetic attitude at all was challenged by George Dickie in 1964, who argued that so-called disinterested attention is just attention, and that the notion does no explanatory work.

Feminist and postcolonial critiques have pressed a different kind of question, asking whose taste the canon encodes, how the category of genius has been distributed, and whether the concept of disinterested contemplation privileges a particular social position with the leisure to contemplate. Linda Nochlin's 1971 essay on why there have been no great women artists reframed the question as one about institutional access, workshop apprenticeship and the life-drawing academy rather than about innate talent, and that reframing has been broadly accepted.

The honest summary is that aesthetics has produced sharp distinctions, powerful partial theories and a much better understanding of why the questions are hard, without producing the consensus that its founders hoped for.

sections.heading: How to Think Aesthetically: A Practical Discipline
sections.body:
Aesthetics is a theoretical subject, but it yields practical guidance for anyone who wants to look, listen and read better, and the guidance is fairly consistent across otherwise opposed theories.

Begin by giving the work time. Museum studies repeatedly find that visitors spend a median of well under thirty seconds per painting, often around seventeen, which is less time than it takes for perception to settle. Almost every aesthetic property discussed by philosophers, balance, tension, unity, expressive quality, requires sustained attention to emerge. Choosing three works and spending ten minutes each will yield more than an hour spent walking past two hundred.

Second, identify the category. Walton's argument that aesthetic properties are category-relative has a direct practical corollary: find out what kind of thing you are looking at before judging it. A work that seems crude may be following conventions you do not know, and a work that seems dazzlingly original may be a competent example of a familiar type. This is the honest content of the demand that criticism be informed, and it is why Hume listed comparison and practice among the marks of a good judge.

Third, separate description from evaluation. Say what is there before saying whether it is good: what materials, what structure, what is repeated, where does the eye or ear go, what is withheld. This discipline slows the reflex of instant verdict and frequently changes it.

Fourth, take your own responses as evidence rather than as conclusions. If a work bores you, ask what it is doing that you are failing to follow; if it moves you, ask what specifically produced that. Both questions are more useful than the verdict they replace, and both are compatible with eventually concluding that a celebrated work is not good.

Fifth, be willing to revise. The strongest empirical regularity in aesthetic response is the mere exposure effect, first systematically demonstrated by Robert Zajonc in 1968: repeated exposure increases liking, particularly for complex stimuli. This means first impressions systematically undervalue difficult work and overvalue immediately fluent work. Works that reward repeated encounter are disproportionately the ones initially resisted.

Sixth, argue, but understand what argument can do. You cannot prove a work good. What you can do, and what criticism at its best does, is direct attention: point to a feature, place the work in a context, propose a category, describe a relation, and invite the other person to look again. Frank Sibley called this perceptual proof, getting someone to see. If they still do not, the conversation has not failed; it has reached the limit Kant identified, where each must judge for themselves.

Finally, remember the field is broader than art. The same attention applied to a hillside, a street, a meal or a conversation is where most aesthetic life actually happens.

guides.title: Epistemology — The Theory of Knowledge
guides.summary: A comprehensive introduction to epistemology, the philosophical study of knowledge: what knowledge is, where it comes from, how beliefs are justified, the major theories and debates, the challenge of skepticism, and the modern branches that extend the field.

sections.heading: What Epistemology Is: The Study of Knowledge
sections.body:
Epistemology is the branch of philosophy that studies knowledge: its nature, its sources, its limits, and the standards by which beliefs count as reasonable. The word derives from the Greek episteme, meaning knowledge or understanding, and logos, meaning account or theory, so epistemology is literally the theory of knowledge. Where metaphysics asks what exists, epistemology asks how, and how well, we can know what exists. It is one of the oldest and most central areas of philosophy, because nearly every other inquiry presupposes that we can distinguish knowing from merely believing, and getting things right from getting them wrong.

Epistemologists concern themselves with several distinct kinds of questions. The most famous is the analysis question: what is knowledge, and what conditions must be met for someone to know something rather than merely believe it? A second is the source question: from what faculties or methods does knowledge arise, and how far can each be trusted, whether perception, memory, reason, testimony, or introspection? A third is the structure question: how are our justified beliefs organized, and what ultimately supports them? A fourth is the value question: why is knowledge more valuable than mere true belief? And a fifth is the skeptical question: can we know anything at all, and how do we answer the challenge that we might be radically deceived?

A useful distinction organizes the field's subject matter. Propositional knowledge, or knowledge-that, is knowledge of facts expressible in a sentence, as in knowing that water is H2O or that Paris is in France. Procedural knowledge, or knowledge-how, is a practical skill, such as knowing how to ride a bicycle or speak a language. Acquaintance knowledge is direct familiarity with a person, place, or sensation. Most of traditional epistemology concentrates on propositional knowledge, because it can be stated, evaluated for truth, and analyzed into components; the theory of skill and the theory of acquaintance are important but more specialized.

Epistemology is normative as well as descriptive. It does not only describe how people happen to form beliefs; it asks how they ought to, which beliefs are rational, which methods are reliable, and what we are entitled to accept on given evidence. In this respect it shades into logic, the philosophy of science, and the study of rationality, and it has practical stakes wherever the quality of belief matters: in courts weighing evidence, in science testing hypotheses, in journalism, medicine, and everyday judgment. Understanding epistemology means learning to ask, of any claim, not merely whether it is true but how one could know, on what basis one believes it, and how confident that basis warrants being. The sections that follow examine each of these questions in turn.

sections.heading: Knowledge as Justified True Belief
sections.body:
For much of the history of philosophy the dominant answer to the question what is knowledge has been the tripartite analysis, often called the justified-true-belief account, or JTB. On this view a person S knows that a proposition p is true if and only if three conditions are jointly satisfied: p is true, S believes that p, and S is justified in believing that p. Each condition rules out a familiar way of falling short of knowledge, and together they were long thought to capture exactly what knowledge is. The account has roots in Plato's dialogues, particularly the Theaetetus, where Socrates explores the idea that knowledge is true belief with an account or reason, though Plato himself raises difficulties for it.

Consider each condition. The truth condition holds that one cannot know something false; if you sincerely believe the earth is flat, you do not know it, because it is not so. Knowledge is factive, meaning it connects the knower to how things actually are. The belief condition holds that knowledge requires belief: you cannot know that p while failing to believe it, since knowing is a way of accepting p as true, not merely encountering the words. There are subtleties here, such as cases where people seem to know without feeling confident, but the core idea is that knowledge is a species of belief. The justification condition holds that mere true belief is not enough. A person who guesses correctly, or who believes something true for a foolish reason, has stumbled on the truth by luck and does not thereby know it. Justification is what distinguishes a well-grounded belief that happens to be true from a lucky guess.

The motivation for the justification condition is easy to feel through examples. Suppose someone believes a lottery ticket will lose purely on a whim, and it does lose; the belief is true, but we hesitate to call it knowledge because it was not held for good reasons. Or suppose a superstitious person believes it will rain because of an aching knee, and it does rain by coincidence; again, true belief without knowledge. Justification is meant to be the ingredient that connects belief to truth in a non-accidental way, so that when one knows, one gets things right not by luck but because one's belief is properly supported.

The JTB account is elegant and intuitive, and for over two thousand years it served as the standard analysis of propositional knowledge. It frames much of the field: theories of justification, debates about sources, and responses to skepticism can all be read as attempts to fill in and defend the three conditions. Yet in the twentieth century a deceptively simple set of counterexamples showed that the three conditions, even together, are not sufficient for knowledge, opening one of modern epistemology's central problems.

sections.heading: The Gettier Problem and the Analysis of Knowledge
sections.body:
In 1963 the American philosopher Edmund Gettier published a three-page paper titled Is Justified True Belief Knowledge? that overturned the settled view. Gettier presented cases in which a person has a belief that is true and justified, yet which we intuitively deny is knowledge, because the belief is true only by a lucky accident that the justification failed to track. These counterexamples showed that the three JTB conditions can all be met while knowledge is absent, so justification, truth, and belief are not jointly sufficient for knowledge.

A standard Gettier case runs as follows. Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get a job and that Jones has ten coins in his pocket, so Smith justifiedly believes the proposition the person who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket. Unknown to Smith, he himself will get the job, and he also, by coincidence, has ten coins in his pocket. Smith's belief is true and was justified, yet it seems wrong to say he knew it, because it turned out true for reasons entirely different from those on which his justification rested. The truth was reached through a stroke of luck that the evidence did not capture. Similar cases can be multiplied endlessly: a person sees what looks like a sheep in a field and truly believes there is a sheep there, but the visible object is a dog and a real sheep is hidden behind it.

Gettier's paper launched a decades-long industry of attempts to repair the analysis of knowledge by adding a fourth condition or replacing justification altogether. One family of responses adds a no-false-lemmas condition, requiring that the belief not be inferred from any false premise; this handles some cases but not all, since Gettier-style examples can be built without inference from falsehoods. Another approach demands defeasibility, that there be no truth which, if known, would undercut the justification. A third invokes causal or tracking conditions, requiring the right sort of connection between the fact and the belief; Robert Nozick, for example, proposed that knowledge requires that one's belief be sensitive, meaning that had p been false one would not have believed it. Reliabilist theories say knowledge is true belief produced by a reliable process.

No proposed fourth condition has won consensus, and after decades some philosophers concluded that knowledge may not be analyzable into simpler necessary and sufficient conditions at all. Timothy Williamson influentially argued that knowledge is a basic, unanalyzable mental state, taking knowledge itself as fundamental rather than built from belief plus additives. Whether or not that view is right, the Gettier problem permanently reshaped epistemology, teaching that ruling out luck is central to knowledge and that the relationship between justification and truth is subtler than the tidy tripartite formula suggested.

sections.heading: The Sources of Knowledge
sections.body:
A second major question asks where knowledge comes from: through what faculties or methods do we acquire justified beliefs, and how far can each be trusted? Traditionally, epistemologists identify several basic sources, each with characteristic powers and vulnerabilities. Understanding them clarifies both how much we know and why our knowledge is fallible.

Perception, knowledge through the senses of sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell, is the richest source of information about the external world and the foundation of empirical inquiry. Yet perception is not a transparent window: illusions, hallucinations, and the theory-ladenness of observation show that the senses can mislead, and philosophers debate whether we perceive objects directly or infer them from inner sensory states. Memory preserves and delivers previously acquired knowledge; without it, knowledge could not accumulate. But memory is reconstructive and fallible, prone to distortion and confabulation, so its deliverances are trusted defeasibly rather than absolutely. Introspection gives each person seemingly privileged access to their own mental states, their pains, beliefs, and sensations. Traditionally regarded as especially secure, introspection too has limits, since people are often mistaken about their own motives and feelings.

Reason, or rational insight, is the source of knowledge that does not depend on sense experience, including logic, mathematics, and conceptual truths. Through reason we grasp that all bachelors are unmarried, that two plus three equals five, and that a valid argument transmits truth from premises to conclusion. Whether reason is a genuine independent source of substantive knowledge, or merely unpacks what is contained in our concepts, is a central dispute between rationalists and empiricists. Testimony, knowledge gained from the words of others, whether in conversation, books, teaching, or news, is the source of the overwhelming majority of what any individual knows. Almost everything you know about history, distant places, science you have not personally verified, and even your own birthdate rests on trusting others. This makes testimony indispensable but also raises hard questions about when trust is warranted, examined by social epistemology.

Epistemologists also debate whether some sources are basic and others derivative. Perception, memory, introspection, and reason are often treated as basic, providing justification non-inferentially, while testimony and inference build upon them, though some argue testimony is itself a basic source. A recurring theme is that no source is infallible: each can and does produce error. Consequently, mature epistemic practice does not rest on any single faculty but cross-checks them against one another, using perception to test testimony, reason to detect inconsistency, and memory to compare present with past. The reliability of our knowledge as a whole emerges less from the perfection of any one source than from the mutual correction of many, a point that connects the study of sources to questions about the very structure of justification.

sections.heading: The Structure of Justification
sections.body:
If our beliefs are justified by other beliefs or by evidence, a natural question arises about how this support is ultimately organized. Suppose you believe p because it is supported by q; but then what supports q? If the answer is another belief r, and r depends on yet another, we face what is called the regress problem: the chain of reasons threatens either to go on forever, to circle back on itself, or to stop somewhere. The major theories of the structure of justification are essentially different answers to this regress.

Foundationalism holds that the regress ends in basic beliefs that are justified but not by further beliefs. These foundational beliefs, perhaps immediate perceptual experiences, simple introspective reports, or self-evident rational truths, provide a bedrock on which all other justified beliefs ultimately rest, like a building standing on a foundation. Classical foundationalists such as Descartes sought foundations that were certain and indubitable; modern moderate foundationalists allow that basic beliefs can be merely prima facie justified and defeasible. The challenge for foundationalism is to explain how any belief can be justified without support from other beliefs, and how the meager foundation of immediate experience can support the vast superstructure of ordinary knowledge.

Coherentism rejects the picture of a one-directional foundation and holds instead that beliefs are justified by their mutual support, by how well they hang together in a coherent system. On this view there are no privileged basic beliefs; justification is holistic, a matter of a belief fitting consistently and explanatorily with the rest of what one believes, like the interlocking pieces of a web or the mutually supporting members of a raft rather than a pyramid on a base. Coherentism explains the interdependence of beliefs well and avoids the awkwardness of self-justifying foundations, but it faces the objection that a system could be internally coherent yet wholly detached from reality, as in a consistent but false story, and the worry that coherence permits vicious circularity.

A third option, infinitism, defended by Peter Klein, bites the bullet and accepts that justification rests on an infinite, non-repeating chain of reasons, arguing that the demand for a terminus or for circularity is what should be rejected. Infinitism is a minority view but sharpens the logical options. Some philosophers pursue hybrid positions, such as foundherentism, associated with Susan Haack, which combines a role for experience with a role for mutual support among beliefs. The debate matters because it concerns whether human knowledge has genuine anchoring in the world or floats as an internally consistent construction, and because different structures imply different diagnoses of where reasoning can go wrong. It also sets the stage for the further question of whether justification is something the knower can access from within, or something that holds in virtue of external facts about reliability.

sections.heading: Internalism, Externalism, and Reliabilism
sections.body:
A deep division in modern epistemology concerns what makes a belief justified, and specifically whether the justifying factors must be accessible to the believer's own reflection. This is the debate between internalism and externalism about justification, and it cuts across the theories of structure discussed earlier.

Internalism holds that the factors determining whether a belief is justified are internal to the believer, in the sense of being accessible through reflection, typically the person's other beliefs, evidence, and conscious mental states. On an internalist view, two people in exactly the same mental condition must be alike in what they are justified in believing, regardless of how the world outside them happens to be arranged. Justification is a matter of having good reasons that one could, at least in principle, cite and examine. This picture fits the intuitive idea that being justified means being responsible and reasonable given one's evidence, and it honors the thought that a person deceived by a convincing illusion is not thereby irrational. The classic worry for internalism is that a subject in a vivid but false experience, or a brain in a vat fed illusory inputs, would count as fully justified even though systematically wrong, so internalist justification seems to guarantee reasonableness without guaranteeing any real link to truth.

Externalism denies that all justifying factors must be internally accessible. On externalist views, whether a belief is justified can depend on facts about the believer's relation to the world that the believer need not be able to recite, above all on whether the belief was produced in a way that reliably yields truth. The leading externalist theory is reliabilism, developed especially by Alvin Goldman, according to which a belief is justified if it is produced by a reliable cognitive process, one that tends to produce true beliefs, such as normal perception, sound memory, or valid inference. A young child or an animal can then have justified beliefs, and knowledge, simply by perceiving reliably, without possessing any theory of why perception is trustworthy. Reliabilism handles many cases naturally and explains why the connection to truth matters, echoing the lesson of the Gettier problem that non-accidental correctness is central.

Externalism faces its own objections. The generality problem asks how to specify the relevant process, since any belief is produced by processes describable at many levels of breadth, with different reliabilities. The new evil demon problem presses that a systematically deceived subject seems justified even though their processes are unreliable in that deceptive world. And critics complain that reliabilism detaches justification from the believer's own perspective, allowing beliefs that are, from the inside, groundless to count as justified so long as they happen to be reliably formed. The internalism-externalism dispute remains unresolved and organizes much contemporary work, with many epistemologists concluding that the term justification may bundle together several distinct notions that different theories rightly capture.

sections.heading: Rationalism, Empiricism, and the A Priori
sections.body:
One of the oldest and most consequential debates in epistemology concerns the ultimate sources of substantive knowledge, and in particular whether the mind can know important truths about reality independently of sense experience. This is the dispute between rationalism and empiricism, and it is bound up with a set of technical distinctions that any student of the subject must master.

Central is the distinction between a priori and a posteriori knowledge. A priori knowledge is knowledge justified independently of experience, graspable by thought alone once the relevant concepts are understood, as in mathematics, logic, and truths like all triangles have three sides. A posteriori, or empirical, knowledge is justified through experience and observation, as in knowing that snow is white or that water boils at a certain temperature. A related distinction, drawn by Immanuel Kant, separates analytic from synthetic propositions: analytic truths are those whose predicate is contained in the subject, true by meaning alone, such as all bachelors are unmarried, whereas synthetic truths say something substantive beyond the mere analysis of concepts.

Rationalists, in a tradition running through Plato, Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz, hold that reason is a source of significant knowledge about reality, and that some of what we know is both a priori and substantive. Descartes sought to rebuild all knowledge on rational foundations discovered by pure thought, and Leibniz held that the necessary truths of mathematics and metaphysics are grasped by the intellect rather than read off the senses. Rationalists often invoke innate ideas or rational intuition and argue that experience alone cannot account for the necessity and universality of mathematical and logical knowledge. Empiricists, in the line of Locke, Berkeley, and Hume, counter that the mind begins as a blank slate and that all our ideas and knowledge derive ultimately from sense experience. Locke attacked innate ideas; Hume argued that any claim about the world beyond present experience, including causation, rests on habit and observation rather than pure reason, and famously drew a sharp line between relations of ideas and matters of fact.

Kant sought a synthesis, arguing that there are synthetic a priori truths, substantive yet knowable independently of experience, made possible because the mind actively structures all experience through built-in forms and categories, so that space, time, and causation are contributed by the knowing subject. In the twentieth century, empiricist logical positivists tried to eliminate the synthetic a priori, treating a priori truths as merely analytic, while W. V. O. Quine, in Two Dogmas of Empiricism, attacked the very analytic-synthetic distinction and argued that no belief is immune from revision in light of experience. The debate persists in new forms, and its stakes are high: it concerns whether human beings can, by thinking, reach truths about the deep structure of reality, or whether all genuine knowledge must ultimately answer to observation.

sections.heading: Skepticism and the Problem of the External World
sections.body:
Skepticism, the view that we lack knowledge, or cannot attain it, in some domain or across the board, is not merely a nuisance but a driving force of epistemology, because meeting the skeptical challenge forces theories of knowledge to justify themselves. Skeptical arguments are powerful precisely because they use ordinary standards of knowledge to reach the extraordinary conclusion that we know almost nothing.

Ancient skepticism took two main forms. Academic skeptics held that knowledge is unattainable, while the Pyrrhonists, following Sextus Empiricus, refused even to assert that, recommending suspension of judgment as the path to tranquility. The Pyrrhonists developed modes, or standard argument patterns, exploiting the conflict of appearances, the relativity of perception, and the regress of justification to show that for any claim an equally strong opposing case can be mounted, so the wise response is to withhold assent. Their goal was practical peace of mind rather than a positive doctrine, a therapeutic rather than merely theoretical skepticism.

Modern skepticism is usually associated with Rene Descartes, who in his Meditations deployed radical doubt as a method. Descartes noted that the senses sometimes deceive, that dreaming can be indistinguishable from waking, and finally imagined an evil demon of great power devoting itself to deceiving him about everything, even simple mathematics. The upshot is the problem of the external world: how can I know that there is a physical world at all, rather than that I am being systematically deceived? Descartes sought to escape by way of the one thing he could not doubt, his own existence as a thinking thing, captured in the cogito, I think therefore I am, and then tried to rebuild knowledge on the guarantee of a non-deceiving God, a move widely regarded as unsuccessful. The modern version replaces the demon with the brain in a vat, a brain kept alive and fed computer-generated experiences indistinguishable from ordinary life; since your experience would be identical whether you are an embodied person or such a brain, how can you rule the second possibility out?

Responses are numerous. G. E. Moore simply insisted that he knew he had hands, treating this as more certain than any skeptical premise, and turned the argument around. Contextualists such as Keith DeRose argue that knowledge is context-sensitive, so that ordinary claims to know are true in everyday contexts while skeptical scenarios raise the standards in the philosophy seminar, dissolving the apparent contradiction. Externalists reply that if our beliefs are in fact reliably produced, we have knowledge whether or not we can refute the skeptic from the inside. Others accept a measure of fallibilism, holding that knowledge does not require the impossibility of error, only that error be suitably ruled out. Few philosophers are genuine global skeptics, but nearly all agree that saying exactly what is wrong with the skeptical argument is far harder than it first appears, which is why skepticism remains a permanent test of every epistemology.

sections.heading: Theories of Truth
sections.body:
Because knowledge requires truth, epistemology is intertwined with the question of what truth itself is. To say a belief is true seems obvious in individual cases, yet philosophers disagree sharply about what truth consists in, and the competing theories carry different implications for how belief connects to the world. This is strictly a topic in metaphysics and the philosophy of language as much as epistemology, but no theory of knowledge is complete without a view about it.

The correspondence theory, the most intuitive and historically dominant, holds that a belief or statement is true when it corresponds to, or matches, the way the world actually is. The statement snow is white is true because, in reality, snow is white; truth is a relation of agreement between a representation and a fact. This theory captures the common-sense idea that truth is about getting reality right and that facts are independent of what anyone believes. Its difficulties lie in specifying what facts are and what the correspondence relation amounts to, especially for negative, general, or abstract truths, and in explaining how we could ever compare a belief with an unconceptualized world.

The coherence theory holds instead that truth consists in a belief's coherence with a comprehensive, consistent system of beliefs. On this view, associated with some idealists such as Bradley and Blanshard, there is no comparing beliefs with a bare reality outside all thought; a belief is true insofar as it fits harmoniously into the maximally coherent whole. Coherence theories connect naturally to coherentist theories of justification but face the objection that more than one internally coherent system might exist, and that coherence seems better suited to being a test of truth than its very nature. The pragmatic theory, developed by Charles Peirce, William James, and John Dewey, ties truth to inquiry and practice: for Peirce, truth is the ideal endpoint on which inquiry would converge, and for James true beliefs are, roughly, those that prove useful and reliable to act upon. Pragmatism usefully links truth to verification and consequence but is criticized for seeming to conflate what is true with what is merely useful to believe.

Deflationary theories take a different tack, denying that truth is a substantive property needing analysis at all. On the redundancy or minimalist view, associated with Frank Ramsey and Paul Horwich, to say it is true that snow is white says no more than that snow is white; the truth predicate is merely a device of endorsement and generalization, letting us affirm claims without restating them. Deflationism dissolves rather than answers the traditional question. The choice among these theories shapes epistemology profoundly, since what one takes truth to be constrains what it could mean for our beliefs to reach it, and whether the goal of inquiry is correspondence to a mind-independent world, coherence within thought, success in practice, or nothing over and above asserting our claims.

sections.heading: Social Epistemology, Testimony, and Disagreement
sections.body:
Traditional epistemology often pictured the knower as a solitary individual, weighing evidence in isolation, but most of what anyone knows depends on other people. Social epistemology studies the collective and interpersonal dimensions of knowledge: how we learn from testimony, how communities and institutions produce and transmit knowledge, and how we should respond when others disagree with us. It has become one of the most active areas of the field, with obvious relevance to science, education, journalism, and public life.

The epistemology of testimony asks when it is rational to believe what others tell us. Since you cannot personally verify most of what you know, from historical facts to scientific results to the reliability of your own name, testimony is indispensable, yet it seems to let you acquire knowledge secondhand. Reductionists, following Hume, argue that trust in testimony is justified only by your own evidence that testimony is generally reliable, so testimonial knowledge reduces to inductive support from experience. Anti-reductionists, following Thomas Reid, counter that testimony is a basic source: we are entitled to believe what we are told unless we have specific reason to doubt it, much as we are entitled to trust perception. Between these lie many nuanced positions, and the debate matters because it determines how demanding rational trust should be and how vulnerable we are to misinformation.

Social epistemology also examines the structures through which knowledge is produced, especially science, treating peer review, replication, expert consensus, and the division of cognitive labor as epistemic institutions whose design affects how reliably truth emerges. It studies the identification of experts by non-experts, a pressing everyday problem, and the epistemic effects of trust, authority, and the internet. A related body of work, feminist and standpoint epistemology, argues that social position and power shape what questions get asked, whose testimony is credited, and what counts as knowledge, and introduces the influential notion of epistemic injustice, developed by Miranda Fricker, whereby people are wronged specifically in their capacity as knowers, for instance when a speaker's credibility is unfairly discounted because of prejudice.

The epistemology of disagreement asks how you should revise your confidence when an epistemic peer, someone equally informed and capable, disagrees with you. Conciliationists argue that peer disagreement should reduce your confidence, since the mere fact that a competent equal reaches the opposite conclusion is evidence you may be mistaken. Steadfast theorists reply that you may rationally retain your view, since you have access to your own reasoning in a way you do not have to the peer's. The question bears directly on intellectual humility, political polarization, and the rationality of holding firm or yielding in the face of dissent. Together these strands show that knowledge is not merely a relation between an individual mind and the world but a social achievement, shaped by trust, testimony, institutions, and the distribution of credibility across a community.

sections.heading: Naturalized, Virtue, and Formal Epistemology
sections.body:
Twentieth- and twenty-first-century epistemology branched into several distinctive programs that reconceive how the theory of knowledge should be pursued. Three of the most influential are naturalized epistemology, virtue epistemology, and formal epistemology, each offering a different vision of the subject.

Naturalized epistemology, launched by W. V. O. Quine in his 1969 essay Epistemology Naturalized, argues that the traditional project of justifying knowledge from an armchair, on purely a priori foundations, has failed, and that epistemology should instead become continuous with empirical science, especially psychology. On this view, we should study how human beings actually form beliefs, how sensory input produces theory, and which cognitive processes are in fact reliable, rather than seeking an impossible foundational certification of knowledge from outside science. Critics object that a purely descriptive study of belief-formation abandons epistemology's essential normative task of saying how we ought to reason, not merely how we do; defenders reply that norms can be recovered from the study of which processes reliably attain our cognitive goals. Naturalism has deeply influenced the field, encouraging attention to cognitive science, evolutionary considerations, and empirical findings about reasoning and bias.

Virtue epistemology shifts the primary focus from the properties of beliefs to the qualities of the believer, taking intellectual virtues as central. Just as virtue ethics evaluates actions by reference to the character of the agent, virtue epistemology evaluates beliefs by reference to the intellectual character of the knower. Reliabilist virtue theorists, such as Ernest Sosa, treat intellectual virtues as stable, reliable cognitive faculties or competences, and analyze knowledge as apt belief, belief that is true because it manifests the knower's competence, an approach that neatly diagnoses Gettier cases as belief that is accurate but not through competence. Responsibilist virtue theorists, such as Linda Zagzebski, emphasize acquired character traits like open-mindedness, intellectual courage, thoroughness, and honesty, connecting epistemology to education and the cultivation of good inquirers. Virtue epistemology has proven fertile for understanding understanding, wisdom, and the value of knowledge.

Formal epistemology brings the tools of logic, probability, and decision theory to bear on epistemic questions, treating degrees of belief, or credences, rather than all-or-nothing belief, as fundamental. Its central framework is Bayesian, representing a rational agent's confidence as probabilities that obey the axioms of the probability calculus and that are updated on new evidence by conditionalization, formalized in Bayes's theorem. This approach illuminates confirmation, evidence, and how much a finding should shift belief, and it underlies much of statistics and the modern philosophy of science. It faces questions about where prior probabilities come from, how idealized rational agents relate to real thinkers, and how graded credence connects to ordinary talk of knowledge and belief. Together, these three programs show epistemology as a living, evolving discipline, drawing on science, ethics, and mathematics rather than resting on a single fixed method.

sections.heading: Misconceptions and Where Epistemology Connects Onward
sections.body:
Several persistent misconceptions distort popular thinking about knowledge, and clearing them away is part of what studying epistemology accomplishes. A first is the confusion of knowledge with certainty. Many assume that to know something one must be absolutely certain, immune from any possibility of error, so that any conceivable doubt shows we do not really know. Most epistemologists reject this: they are fallibilists, holding that one can know something while it remains logically possible that one is mistaken, since requiring certainty would collapse into the very skepticism the equation was meant to avoid. Knowledge asks for adequate grounding and non-accidental truth, not the impossibility of error.

A second misconception treats all opinions as epistemically equal, sliding from the true observation that people disagree to the false conclusion that no belief is better justified than another. Epistemology is precisely the study of the standards that make some beliefs more reasonable, better supported, and more likely true than others; recognizing fallibility is not the same as embracing a relativism in which evidence and argument make no difference. A third confuses the psychological question of what causes a belief with the normative question of what justifies it: that a belief was produced by upbringing or emotion neither guarantees nor precludes that it is well justified, and the genetic origin of a belief must be separated from its rational credentials. A fourth mistakes knowing-that for knowing-how, or assumes that being able to state a rule is the same as possessing a skill, when the two can come apart entirely.

Properly understood, epistemology is not idle wordplay but a discipline with pervasive practical stakes. It underwrites the philosophy of science, which asks how evidence confirms theories and what makes a method rational, and it shapes debates about expertise, testimony, and misinformation that determine how a society sustains reliable belief. It informs law, where standards of proof, the weighing of testimony, and reasonable doubt are epistemic notions; medicine, where diagnosis is inference under uncertainty; and education, whose aim is the cultivation of good inquirers. In an age of information overload, algorithmic curation, and coordinated deception, the epistemological questions of when to trust a source, how to weigh conflicting evidence, and how confident to be have become urgently practical.

Epistemology also connects to the rest of philosophy. It borders metaphysics through the question of truth and the nature of the reality we seek to know; it borders ethics through the norms of belief, intellectual virtue, and the responsibilities of the inquirer; it borders logic and the philosophy of mind through the analysis of reasoning, evidence, and mental states; and it borders the philosophy of language through the vehicles by which knowledge is expressed and communicated. To think clearly about knowledge, in the end, is to learn to ask of any claim not only whether it is true but how one could know, on what basis one believes it, and how much confidence that basis can bear, a habit of mind that is among the most valuable philosophy can teach.

guides.title: Metaphysics — The Study of What Exists
guides.summary: An introduction to metaphysics, the branch of philosophy that asks what fundamentally exists and what reality is like: its history, its central problems of being, universals, identity, causation, time, freedom, possibility and mind, and the criticisms it has faced.

sections.heading: What Metaphysics Is and Its Place in Philosophy
sections.body: Metaphysics is the branch of philosophy that inquires into the most fundamental nature of reality: what there is, what it is like at bottom, and what the most general features of existence are. Where the special sciences each study some particular domain, physics the physical, biology the living, economics the exchange of goods, metaphysics asks questions that lie beneath and across all of them. It asks not what particular things exist but what it is for anything to exist at all; not what causes a specific event but what causation itself is; not whether a given object has changed but what change and persistence are. These are questions that no experiment can straightforwardly settle, because they concern the framework within which experiments are interpreted rather than any measurable quantity, and yet they are unavoidable the moment one begins to think carefully about the world. A helpful way to grasp the subject is through its classic questions. Do numbers exist, or only the things we count? When a river flows on and every drop is replaced, in what sense is it the same river? Is the future already fixed, or genuinely open? Are you the same person you were as a child, and what makes you so? Could things have been otherwise than they are, and what grounds such possibilities? Is the mind simply the brain, or something more? Each of these is a metaphysical question, and each has been debated for millennia without the kind of consensus that mature sciences achieve, which is part of what makes metaphysics both frustrating and perennially alive. Metaphysics sits alongside the other great divisions of philosophy and is intertwined with them. Epistemology asks how and whether we can know things; metaphysics asks what there is to be known. Logic supplies the tools of valid inference that metaphysical arguments must respect. Ethics and aesthetics presuppose metaphysical views about persons, values and freedom. Because metaphysics concerns the most general structure of reality, its conclusions ripple outward into every other area of thought, which is why thinkers as different as Plato, Aristotle, Aquinas, Descartes, Leibniz, Hume and Kant all found they could not avoid it. The word itself, as the next section explains, arose from an accident of editing, but the enterprise it names is as old as systematic thought.
